subsection: 2. Floors, walls, furniture and soft furnishings

notes.h: Floor structures and what they mean for the covering
notes.b: Before choosing a floor covering you need to know what lies beneath it, because the structure decides what the covering has to cope with. There are two structures: solid and suspended.
points: A solid floor is a concrete slab laid on hardcore (a layer of broken stone) with a damp-proof layer (a membrane or course) to stop moisture rising, and finished with a thin screed (a smooth fine-concrete top coat). It is usually found on the ground floor of modern homes.

A suspended floor is made of joists (timber, concrete or steel beams) carrying tongue-and-groove boards or planks, with an air space beneath. The air circulates and lets moisture escape, so the boards stay dry. It is usually found on upper floors.
A damp-proof course (a waterproof layer) can be added in a suspended floor to prevent dampness reaching the boards.

Boards in a suspended floor can be sanded and varnished. Gaps and loose boards in a suspended timber floor must be fixed before a new covering is laid, because they would show through and make the covering uneven.
Diagram: draw cross-sections of both floors. For the solid floor label the screed, concrete slab, damp-proof layer and hardcore. For the suspended floor label the boards, joists and air space.
notes.tip: Students often reverse these. Solid means concrete on the ground floor. Suspended means joists and boards with an air space, usually upstairs. When asked to explain each, give the materials, the usual location and how dampness is prevented.

notes.b: Floor coverings are grouped as hard, semi-hard and soft. Hard coverings include clay and stone tiles, glass and resin mosaics and safety vinyl, so they last well and clean easily, but they tend to be cold and unforgiving underfoot.
points: Ceramic tiles are made from clay, minerals and water, can be glazed or unglazed, and come in many sizes and shapes. Terracotta and glazed stone tiles are related tile types.
Ceramic tiles are hard-wearing, easy to clean, stain resistant and resistant to water, so they suit wet areas. They are cold and hard underfoot and can crack or chip if something heavy falls on them.
Quarry tiles are unglazed clay tiles that are hard-wearing, which is why they suit hallways and kitchens.
Flagstones are cut natural stone with uneven textures and natural colours, such as in a hallway. They are hard-wearing but cold underfoot and chip easily.
Slate is a fine-grained, foliated (layered) metamorphic rock. Its main points are that it is hard-wearing and easy to clean. It is also warm underfoot and slightly absorbent.
Marble and travertine are natural limestone-type stone, refined and cut into tiles and slabs, with flecks of colour. They are attractive but chip easily and are cold underfoot.

Stone carpeting is a gravel-based mixture poured on the subfloor and sealed when set. Mosaics are made of glass, metal, resin and stone in varied textures and colours, and are decorative and hard-wearing.
Safety flooring is a slip-resistant vinyl covering, used where slipping is a risk such as in bathrooms and hospitals. It is also hard-wearing and hygienic.
notes.tip: A description question wants the name, what it is made of, two properties, and an advantage and a disadvantage. Marble and travertine are cut natural stone, not manufactured, and slate is given as warm underfoot.

notes.b: Semi-hard coverings, such as wood, vinyl, linoleum, cork, coir and sisal, are firm but have more give than tile or stone. Each is chosen for particular properties, so learn what each is made of and its main strength and weakness.
points: Strip wood flooring is made of tongue-and-groove strips of hardwood such as oak, beech or maple, or softwood such as pine or spruce. It may be solid.
Block parquet is made of hardwood blocks laid in a herringbone pattern, and mosaic parquet uses blocks laid in a basket-weave pattern.
Wood flooring is attractive, durable and low maintenance, and most boards are sold ready sealed, so they need little finishing. It can be expensive.
Wood flooring is noisy, cold underfoot, and marked or scratched easily. Softwood boards dent more readily than hardwood.
Laminated wood flooring is laminated, with a plastic veneer (a thin surface layer) over the wood. It is hard-wearing and low maintenance, but hard underfoot and may scratch.

Vinyl is made from polyvinyl chloride (PVC), a plastic developed from petroleum, mixed with resin, plasticiser, pigment and filler, and put together under heat and pressure on a backing. It comes in sheets or tiles in many colours and designs, such as marbled, flecked, embossed, veined or striped.
Vinyl is durable (varying with thickness), quiet, easy to clean, hygienic, stain resistant and resistant to water, acids and alkalis. It can be marked by heels or furniture.
Foam-backed vinyl is softer and warmer underfoot because of its foam layer, but vinyl may scorch or melt if exposed to high heat.
notes.tip: Strip wood, parquet and mosaic parquet are three different layouts, so name the pattern (herringbone for block parquet, basket weave for mosaic). For vinyl, always give a weakness as well, that it melts or scorches with heat.

notes.b: These four coverings are made from natural plant materials. Each has a different set of properties, so do not give one the properties of another.
points: Linoleum is a natural floor covering made from linseed oil, cork dust and resin on a jute backing. It is resilient (springs back after pressure), quiet underfoot and easy to care for.

Cork is made from granules of the bark of the cork oak bonded with polyurethane resin, or sliced directly from the bark. It is sold sealed or unsealed, and is warm and quiet underfoot but not very hard-wearing.
Coir is made from coconut fibre that is softened in water, beaten, spun and woven. It is tough and hard-wearing.
Sisal is made from the fibre of an agave plant, a dark green spiky plant. It is hard-wearing, easy to clean and anti-static (it does not build up static electricity).
notes.tip: Coir is tough and hard-wearing but not easy to clean. Give easy to clean to sisal only.

notes.b: Soft coverings are carpets and rugs. They are the warmest and quietest choice underfoot, but they need more care than hard floors.
points: Carpet is soft, warm and resilient underfoot, insulates against heat and absorbs sound. It comes in many colours and patterns and is durable.
Carpet needs regular vacuuming because it dirties easily, and it can be expensive, depending on fibre and quality.
Woven carpets have a fabric pile woven onto a hessian backing. Axminster has a cut pile and allows an almost unlimited range of colours and designs.
Wilton is woven from a continuous strand of yarn. It is thicker than Axminster but limits the number of colours.
Tufted carpets have tufts inserted into a woven backing, held in place with adhesive and usually backed with foam.
Fibre blends include 100 per cent wool, acrylic and polypropylene. Carpets made of 80 per cent wool and 20 per cent nylon combine the warmth and resilience of wool with the durability of nylon.

Carpet tiles are sealed-edge squares backed with PVC or rubber and are stain resistant. A damaged tile can be replaced individually, but the range of colours and patterns is limited. They are graded light, medium, heavy and general.

Underlay sits beneath carpet, so it adds cushioning and insulation and extending the life of the carpet. Rugs are loose and can be moved, but they need a non-slip backing to prevent slipping on hard floors.
notes.tip: Axminster is cut pile with unlimited colours, while Wilton is a continuous strand with limited colours and is thicker. Do not say carpet is always dearer than hard floors; say it can be expensive.

notes.b: The right covering depends on the room it is going into and the people who use it, so work through a set of factors. Each factor needs a reason when you answer a question.
points: Function and traffic flow decide durability: hallways and kitchens need hard-wearing surfaces, while bedrooms can take soft coverings.
Subfloor condition and type must be checked, as a poor subfloor will show through thin coverings and make laying difficult.
Warmth underfoot matters in bedrooms and bathrooms. Cold surfaces such as tile or stone can be made warmer with underfloor heating or rugs.
Maintenance, cleaning and hygiene: a sealed or non-porous covering is easier to keep clean than an unsealed one.
Noise is reduced by soft coverings and by underlay, which is important in flats and upper-floor rooms. Safety also counts, so a non-slip surface suits wet areas.
Cost includes the purchase price, laying and upkeep, so a cheaper covering that needs frequent replacement may cost more over time.
Décor, the size of the room, the flooring in adjoining rooms and the occupants also influence the choice.

Typical matches: hallway (ceramic, quarry tile, flagstone, wood or vinyl); kitchen (tiles, vinyl or linoleum); bathroom (ceramic, slate, vinyl or safety flooring, which are durable, water resistant and non-slip); sitting room (wood, carpet or vinyl); bedroom (carpet); home office (carpet or carpet tiles).
notes.tip: When asked to recommend a covering for a named room, give the covering and then reasons such as durable, water resistant, non-slip, warm, easy to clean or sound-absorbent, as relevant to that room. Give one reason for each factor you name.

notes.b: Paint is the most common wall finish because it is cheap and quick to apply. The main choice is between water-based and solvent-based paint, and between finishes that reflect light and ones that absorb it.
points: Emulsion paint is water-based, quick drying, easy to apply, low odour and inexpensive, and is available in a wide variety of colours and shades. It is durable and washable.
Silk vinyl emulsion is a washable emulsion with a slight sheen, suitable for children's rooms, kitchens and hallways.

Solvent-based gloss or satin paint is hard-wearing and washable and copes with high condensation, so it is often used on woodwork and in kitchens and bathrooms. It has a strong smell and dries slowly.
Gloss paint reflects light and is washable. Matt paint absorbs light and hides surface flaws, but it marks more easily and is harder to wipe clean.
Textured paint contains plastic fibres that create a rough, textured finish. Specialised paints include flame retardant paint and mould resistant paint for bathrooms.
notes.tip: Students reverse these. Gloss and silk reflect light and wipe clean, while matt absorbs light and hides flaws but marks more easily.

notes.h: Wall finishes: wallpaper, tiles and other finishes
notes.b: Where paint is not enough, a wall can be papered, tiled, panelled or decorated. Each choice suits different rooms and conditions.
points: General-purpose wallpaper has a design printed on paper, varies in thickness and hides faults. Embossed wallpaper has a design stamped into the paper and can be painted.
Woodchip wallpaper is paper with wood chips in it, hides faults and can be painted. Flock wallpaper has a raised, velvet-like pattern.

Vinyl or washable wallpaper is plastic-coated, so it is washable, strong and hard-wearing and withstands condensation. It has a huge choice of designs, camouflages faults, can be patterned or textured and makes rooms cosier.
Lining paper is a plain paper applied before paint or wallpaper to give a smooth, even surface.

Ceramic or porcelain wall tiles are waterproof, easy to clean and hygienic, which makes them suitable behind sinks and cookers, around baths and in showers. They come glazed or unglazed in many colours, sizes and patterns.
Tiling needs a sound wall, waterproof adhesive and grout (the filler between tiles). It is costly to install and can feel cold.
Panelling in wood or medium-density fibreboard adds texture and warmth to a wall, such as in a living room.
Stencils and motifs can be added to a painted wall to add decoration.
notes.tip: Name each wallpaper type and give two properties. Matches to know: a child's bedroom takes silk vinyl emulsion (washable, easy to apply, quick drying, inexpensive, motifs and stencils can be added); kitchen and bathroom suit tiles, washable vinyl paint or vinyl wallpaper; a living room suits water-based or textured paint, or washable or embossed wallpaper.

notes.b: Choosing a wall finish means matching it to the room's conditions, the people using it and the budget. Give a reason with each factor.
points: The function of the room and its conditions decide the finish: a hallway needs a washable surface, a kitchen or bathroom has moisture, while a bedroom can have a matt, softer finish.
Durability depends on traffic flow and the age of the occupants, since young children are more likely to mark walls. Non-toxic products matter in children's rooms.
The size and shape of a room and the condition of its walls affect the choice. Cracks, damp or uneven plaster must be treated, and damaged walls may need filling or lining before decoration.
Light reflectance: gloss and pale finishes reflect light and brighten a room, while matt and dark finishes absorb it.
Maintenance and cleaning: a washable finish saves time and cost over the life of the wall.
Budget must cover materials, preparation and professional labour, which adds to the cost of tiling and wallpapering.
Environmental impact: water-based paints release fewer volatile organic compounds (harmful vapours given off as paint dries) than solvent-based paints.
Décor and trends, texture and finish, ease of application, coverage and aesthetics (how the finish looks) also affect the choice.
notes.tip: Examiners expect one reason for each factor you give. The commonly asked factors are function, décor, durability, size and condition of walls, maintenance, budget and light reflectance.

notes.b: Furniture is expensive and used for years, so choose it with several factors in mind. Think about the room, the user and the cost.
points: Furniture style may be antique, traditional or contemporary, and the choice should suit the room's décor and the occupants' preferences. The function of the room and the principles of design, such as proportion and balance, also matter.
Space available determines the size of each piece, so the room, doors and stairs should be measured before purchase.
Freestanding furniture can be moved and replaced easily, while built-in units make best use of alcoves and awkward spaces.
Comfort and ergonomics (how well a piece fits the human body): seat height and depth should suit the people who will use the furniture. Adjustable furniture suits people with special needs.
Construction and quality: the frame, joints and fixings show how long a piece will last, and solid timber is more durable than chipboard. Durability and safety also count.

Safety labels, quality marks and guarantees indicate that a product has been tested and is backed by the manufacturer. Choose furniture and upholstery that is fire resistant and carries safety labels.
Budget: a well-made piece costs more initially but lasts longer, so cost must be weighed against quality. Availability also matters.
For a bedroom, consider storage, size, durability and safety. For an office, consider desk size and shape, the chair, built-in drawers and shelving, with both functional and aesthetic guidelines.
notes.tip: Factor questions for a bedroom, office or living room are common. Give each factor with a reason, such as measuring doors and stairs so the piece fits, or solid timber lasting longer than chipboard.

notes.b: Storage furniture holds belongings and keeps a room usable. The types differ in how fixed, flexible and costly they are.
points: Storage furniture includes wall units, filing cabinets, TV cabinets, furniture chests, toy boxes and storage boxes and baskets.
Built-in wardrobes have hanging rails, drawers and shelving and are custom built to suit the space, but they cannot be moved.
Shelving and bookcases are open, so items are easy to see, and cheap, and may be made of wood or metal.
Modular units (separate sections that fit together) can be combined in different arrangements, such as a wall unit with shelving, cupboards, a display area or a desk. They suit confined spaces.
Flat-pack furniture is supplied in parts for home assembly and is usually cheaper. Free-standing flat-pack units are common.
Storage keeps a room tidy, conceals clutter and makes items easy to find.
Display shelves show photographs, trophies and ornaments, which enhances the appearance of a room.
notes.tip: When asked to name and describe items of storage furniture, give each item with a reason for choosing it, such as avoiding clutter, concealing items, displaying photographs and trophies, finding items easily or improving the room's appearance.

notes.b: Soft furnishings are the fabric items that make a room comfortable and give it character. The fabric must suit each item's job, so the properties needed differ.
points: Soft furnishings include curtains, blinds, cushions, throws, rugs, bed linen and upholstery fabrics, as well as bean bags, pouffes, lamp shades and arm covers.
Curtain fabric should drape well and be pre-shrunk, fade resistant and flame resistant, and it should be durable enough for repeated opening and closing.
Lined curtains insulate a window and stop draughts, which reduces heat loss from a room. They also give privacy and can add width to a window.
Roller blinds roll up neatly and suit small windows. Venetian blinds have adjustable slats that control the amount of light and privacy. Blinds also suit roof (Velux) windows.
Cushion fabric should be strong, cleanable and stain resistant, so that it survives constant use and spills.
Bed linen should be smooth, closely woven, absorbent, easy to launder and shrink resistant, so it feels comfortable and washes repeatedly.

Upholstery fabric (the covering on seats and sofas) should be durable, comfortable, resilient, stain resistant and hard-wearing. Fabrics named in marking schemes include cotton, linen, wool, polyester, velvet and silk.
Soft furnishings add colour, pattern and texture, create warmth, comfort and cosiness, form focal points, give privacy and insulation, and update a room's style economically.
notes.tip: When asked to recommend soft furnishings, name the item, the fabric and the property that suits its use. Link each answer to how it improves the room.

keyTerms.definition: A concrete slab laid on hardcore with a damp-proof membrane and a screed finish, usually found at ground level in modern homes.
A floor of joists carrying boards, with an air space beneath that prevents dampness, usually found on upper floors.
A hard-wearing, easy-to-clean floor covering made from polyvinyl chloride, a plastic developed from petroleum.
A layer laid beneath carpet that adds cushioning and insulation and extends the life of the carpet.
A sealed-edge square of carpet backed with PVC or rubber, which can be replaced individually if damaged.
A plain paper applied to a wall before decoration to provide a smooth, even surface.
A washable water-based paint with a slight sheen, suitable for rooms that need frequent cleaning.
A blind with adjustable horizontal slats that control the amount of light and privacy in a room.

factCards.term: Three hard floor coverings with a property each
factCards.definition: Ceramic tiles are hard-wearing and easy to clean; slate is hard-wearing and warm underfoot; marble chips easily and is cold underfoot.
Carpet and carpet tiles. Both are soft and warm underfoot and absorb sound.
Durable, low maintenance and attractive, but noisy, cold underfoot and easily scratched.

factCards.term: Four factors when choosing wall finishes
factCards.definition: Function of the room, durability, washability and cost.

factCards.term: Two things lined curtains do for a window
factCards.definition: They insulate the window and stop draughts.

factCards.term: Three ways soft furnishings enhance a room
factCards.definition: They add colour, pattern and texture; create warmth and cosiness; and update the room's style at low cost.

questions.prompt: Name one hard and one soft floor covering suitable for a bedroom, and give one property of each.
questions.model: Hard floor covering named with one property (3 marks): laminated wood flooring, hard-wearing and low maintenance; or vinyl, durable and easy to clean. Soft floor covering named with one property (3 marks): carpet, soft and warm underfoot and absorbs sound; or carpet tiles, warm and replaceable individually.

questions.prompt: A young couple are furnishing the living room of a house with a suspended timber floor. The room will also be used as a play area for a toddler. Recommend a floor covering and a wall finish for the room, and justify each recommendation with reference to durability, safety, cost and maintenance.
questions.model: Floor covering (up to 8 marks): a covering suited to a suspended timber floor, such as carpet on underlay or a laminated or engineered wood covering, with the subfloor checked first for gaps and loose boards; justification refers to warmth and softness for a toddler, a soft surface reducing injury from falls, sound absorption, cost of purchase and laying, and ease of cleaning spills and stains. Wall finish (up to 8 marks): a washable silk vinyl emulsion or vinyl wallpaper, which resists marking and can be wiped clean; justification refers to durability against a toddler's handling, low cost compared with tile, easy application, and a matt or pale finish that suits the room's light. Overall decision (up to 2 marks): the recommendations are consistent with the function of the room and the budget.
